course.title: Plumbing: How Water Gets In and Out of a House
course.lead: A free, self-paced course on the whole plumbing system: water in under pressure, waste out by gravity, and everything between. Learn what each part does, how they fit together, how to tell when something’s wrong, what you can safely fix yourself, and when to call a licensed plumber.
how: Start with Lesson 1 for the big picture, then go in order or jump to the part of the house you’re curious about.
Each lesson has labeled diagrams, a parts table where it fits, a short quiz and links to go deeper. Badges show the level.
Play with the interactive pieces: the pressure tower, the trap and vent, the animated toilet, the water heater and the leak counter.
Use the troubleshooting finder when something seems wrong, and climb the skill ladder one rung at a time.
course.who: Written for teens and adults with no plumbing experience. It picks up where the house guides in Being an Adult 101 leave off.
course.why: Each lesson explains the “why” as well as the “what”: why a foot of water adds 0.433 psi, why a 2-inch trap seal needs a vent, why freezing water splits pipes, why a tankless heater needs so much power. Facts and numbers come from U.S. government agencies such as EPA, CDC, DOE, HUD, CPSC, USGS and BLS, from university extension programs and OpenStax textbooks, and every lesson lists its sources.
course.final: Your local code and the authority having jurisdiction have the final word. This course explains how plumbing works in general. Manufacturers’ instructions come first for their products.

lessons.title: The Big Picture
lessons.short: Water comes in under pressure and leaves by gravity: a map of a house’s plumbing.
lessons.intro: A house has two plumbing systems that must never mix. One brings clean water in under pressure. The other carries used water and waste away by gravity, with vents that let air in. This lesson gives you the map; every later lesson zooms in on one part of it.

blocks.h: Two systems: pressure in, gravity out
blocks.html:
The supply system is a closed web of small pipes that stays full of water all the time. The water in it is under pressure, pushed by a pump or by water stored high up in a tank or tower. That push is what lifts water to a second-floor shower and makes it spray out of a faucet the moment you open it.

The drain-waste-vent system, or DWV, works the other way. Its pipes are bigger, they run only partly full, and nothing pushes the water along. Every drain slopes downhill and lets gravity do the work. Vent pipes connect the drains to the open air above the roof so air can move in and out as water rushes past.

The two systems must stay apart. HUD’s federal standard for manufactured homes puts it plainly: no part of the water system may be connected to drainage or vent piping. Plumbing codes for other homes have the same goal, because a connection could let sewage get pulled back into the water you drink (Lesson 2 explains how that can happen).

blocks.h: Where the water comes from, and where it goes
blocks.html:
Most homes get water from a public system. The U.S. Geological Survey says about 87 percent of Americans get their water from a public supply. The utility treats the water, tests it, and pushes it through mains under the street. Most of the rest rely on a private well with a pump. With a well, the owner is in charge: the CDC notes that government officials do not regulate, treat or monitor water from private wells, so testing it is up to you (Lesson 7).

Used water leaves the same two ways. In towns it flows into a public sewer that carries it to a treatment plant. In the country it often goes to a septic system: a buried tank where solids settle out, and a drainfield where the soil treats the liquid (Lesson 3).

blocks.html:
The pipe that carries water from the public main to a building is called the service line. Near the street there’s usually a valve called the curb stop, and HUD’s inspection guide notes it is usually the water department’s responsibility. Being an Adult 101 gives the rule of thumb: leave the valve at the meter or property line to your water utility or a licensed plumber, and learn to use the main shutoff inside your home (Shut Off Your Home’s Water).

Inside the house, the plumbing belongs to the owner, and so does the job of keeping it working.

Many jobs need a permit and an inspection, and some work must be done by a licensed plumber. Where this course quotes a code, it’s an example; your local code may differ.

quiz.q: What moves water through the supply pipes?
opts: Pressure from a pump or from water stored up high
quiz.why: Supply pipes are full and pressurized, pushed by a pump or by the height of water in a tank or tower.

quiz.q: What moves water through the drains?

quiz.q: About what share of Americans get water from a public supply, according to USGS?

lessons.title: Water Supply: From the Street to the Faucet
lessons.short: The service line, meter and main shutoff; where water pressure comes from; pressure-reducing valves, pipe sizes, water hammer and backflow.
lessons.intro: Follow a gallon of water from the main under the street to your kitchen faucet. Along the way you’ll meet the valves that control it, the physics that pushes it, and the devices that keep the pressure safe and the water clean.

blocks.h: From the main to the house
blocks.html:
A water main runs under the street. The U.S. Army’s plumbing manual describes mains as usually cast iron and 8 inches or more across. A plumber taps a small valve, the corporation stop, into the main, and the house’s service line runs from it toward the house. The Army manual gives three-quarters of an inch as the smallest practical size for a service line.

Near the property line is the curb stop, a valve set in a stop box so it can be reached from the surface. Next comes the meter, which measures how much water you use, either in a pit near the street or inside the house. Then, where the line comes through the wall, your home’s main shutoff valve. Close it and no new water can get in anywhere (Shut Off Your Home’s Water).

After the main shutoff, many homes have a pressure-reducing valve. Then the cold line branches out to every fixture, and one branch feeds the water heater. Hot water leaves the heater in pipes that run alongside the cold ones.

blocks.html:
Pressure is force spread over an area. In a liquid at rest, the pressure grows with depth, because the water underneath has to hold up the weight of all the water above it. OpenStax’s physics textbook gives the rule as P = hρg: pressure equals depth times density times the pull of gravity. The width of the container doesn’t matter; only the height of the water does.

That’s why towns put water in tall towers and hilltop tanks, and why pumps push it up into them. A faucet 100 feet below the water’s surface in a tower feels the weight of a 100-foot column of water.

In U.S. units, the numbers work out neatly. NIST gives the pressure under one foot of water as 2,988.98 pascals and one psi as 6,894.757 pascals, so each foot of height adds about 0.433 psi. A faucet 115 feet below the water level gets about 50 psi. Climb 10 feet, about one story, and you lose a bit more than 4 psi. The Army manual puts pressure in a main usually between 45 and 60 psi.

A pressure gauge on a hose bibb reads gauge pressure: the pressure above the air pressure all around us. That’s the number plumbers and codes use.

P = h × ρ × g
1 foot of water: 2,988.98 Pa ÷ 6,894.757 Pa per psi ≈ 0.433 psi
pressure (psi) ≈ 0.433 × height of water above the tap (feet)

blocks.cap: Drag the water level in the tower, change the ground level of the house, or add a pressure-reducing valve. Gauges show static pressure: the pressure with no water flowing. Real pressure while water flows is lower, because friction in the pipes uses some of it up.

blocks.h: Too much pressure: the pressure-reducing valve
blocks.html:
Low ground means high pressure. The City of Edmond, Oklahoma, offers an elevation lookup for that reason: addresses below 1,150 feet automatically need a pressure-reducing valve. Edmond quotes the model code it enforces, the 2018 International Residential Code, section P2903.3.1: “The static water pressure shall be not greater than 80 psi (551 kPa).” Where the main’s pressure is higher, an approved pressure-reducing valve “shall be installed” where the water service enters. HUD’s standard for manufactured homes uses the same 80 psi line. That is the model code; your local code may differ.

A pressure-reducing valve, or PRV, uses a spring and a diaphragm to let water through only until the pressure on the house side reaches its setting. San Diego’s utility guidelines call for setting a new PRV between 45 and 75 psi. It lists signs that a PRV is failing: banging or a high-pitched whistle in the pipes, often when water is turned off; more flow and pressure at faucets than you’d expect; and frequent leaks in toilets and faucets.

EPA’s WaterSense home maintenance checklist says to check your service water pressure once a year and adjust or replace the pressure-regulating valve if needed.

A simple pressure gauge threads onto an outdoor hose bibb or a laundry faucet. With no water running anywhere in the house, open the faucet and read it. That’s your static pressure. If it’s over 80 psi, talk to a licensed plumber about a PRV. Replacing a PRV means cutting into the main line, so check whether your town requires a permit or a licensed plumber.

blocks.h: Pressure isn’t the same as flow
blocks.html:
Pressure is the push. Flow rate is how much water actually comes out each minute. OpenStax defines it as the volume that passes a point per unit of time, and shows that flow equals the pipe’s cross-section area times the average speed of the water (Q = A v).

Moving water rubs against the pipe walls, so some pressure is used up along the way. In smooth, slow flow, OpenStax’s Poiseuille’s law shows the resistance growing with the pipe’s length and falling with the fourth power of its radius. Halve a pipe’s radius and its resistance goes up 16 times. That’s why a long run of small pipe can feel weak at the far end, and why the main lines are bigger than the branches.

HUD’s inspection guide gives a quick check: a kitchen faucet should fill a one-gallon jug in about 24 seconds. That’s 2.5 gallons per minute. The same guide calls 15 psi at each fixture, with water flowing, preferable, and 8 psi the least that will do.

flow rate: Q = A × v  (area × average speed)
laminar resistance: R = 8ηl ÷ (πr⁴)  (longer or thinner pipe → more resistance)

blocks.h: Hot and cold side by side
blocks.html:
The hot water system runs alongside the cold, from the water heater to every fixture that needs hot water. Hot is on the left: HUD’s manufactured home standard, for example, requires faucets to deliver hot water from the left-hand side, the familiar arrangement in most homes.

Hot water cools in the pipes between uses, so a faucet far from the heater runs cold for a while first. The Army manual describes the fix used in bigger buildings: a two-pipe system that keeps hot water circulating. Some newer homes use manifold plumbing instead, with a separate line from a central manifold to each fixture. The Department of Energy notes that fewer joints mean fewer leaks, and one line can be shut off without turning off the rest (Lesson 5).

Moving water is heavy. Stop it all at once, as a quick-closing valve does, and it slams to a halt with a bang. The Army manual calls this water hammer and lists the effects: noise, rattling pipes and sometimes leaky joints. The classic fix is an air chamber: a capped pipe near the valve that holds a cushion of air. Air squeezes and water doesn’t, so the air works like a car’s shock absorber. Lesson 9 has a diagram.

A cross-connection is any point where something that isn’t drinking water could come into contact with the drinking water. Water in a pipe normally flows one way, but if the supply pressure drops, water can be pulled backward, and with it whatever the end of a hose or a faucet is sitting in.

Plumbing systems block that path in several ways. An air gap is the simplest: the spout ends well above the rim of the sink or tub, so nothing can be sucked back up. A vacuum breaker lets air into the line when the pressure drops, which breaks the siphon. HUD’s manufactured home standard, as one example, requires a listed nonremovable backflow device on outdoor hose bibbs, a fixed air gap inside dishwashers and clothes washers, and vacuum breakers mounted at least 6 inches above the fixture’s flood level on flush valves.

lessons.title: Drains, Traps and Vents
lessons.short: Gravity and slope, the trap’s water seal, why vents keep traps from siphoning, cleanouts, the building sewer and septic systems.
lessons.intro: Drains look simple: water goes down. But a drain system has a hidden job. It has to carry waste away while blocking sewer gas from coming back up, and it does that with nothing more than a bend of pipe, a little water, and a pipe through the roof.

blocks.html:
Nothing pushes water through a drain. Each horizontal pipe slopes gently downhill so gravity carries water and solids along. Too flat, and solids settle out; the Army manual and HUD’s standard for manufactured homes both use a quarter inch of fall for every foot of pipe. HUD allows an eighth of an inch per foot only where a quarter inch isn’t practical, and then only with a full-size cleanout at the upper end. The model code where you live sets the exact slopes for each pipe size.

A quarter inch per foot doesn’t sound like much, but it adds up. A 20-foot run falls 5 inches.
fall = slope × run    20 ft × ¼ in per ft = 5 in  (about a 2 percent grade)

blocks.h: The trap and its water seal
blocks.html:
Sewers are full of gases that smell bad and can be harmful. If a sink drain ran straight down to the sewer, those gases would flow right up into the room. The fix is the trap: a U-shaped bend under every fixture that stays full of water after the fixture drains. HUD’s inspection guide describes it as designed to hold a water seal that blocks sewer gas from coming up through the drain.

The seal depth is the height of water between the low point of the top of the bend (the dip) and the lip where water spills out (the weir). HUD’s manufactured home standard calls for P-traps with a seal of 2 to 4 inches. It also bans S-traps, drum traps and bell traps, and HUD’s inspection guide explains why S-traps are no longer allowed by plumbing codes: they tend to siphon themselves dry.

A trap is a pressure gauge in disguise. A seal 2 inches deep can hold back a pressure difference of 2 inches of water. NIST puts an inch of water at about 249 pascals, so a 2-inch seal resists only about 0.07 psi (0.5 kPa), hundreds of times less than the pressure in your supply pipes. Tiny pressure changes in the drain can push or pull that water out. That’s the job of the vent.

blocks.html:
When a slug of water rushes down a drain, it acts like a piston. Ahead of it, air is pushed; behind it, air is pulled. Without a way for air to get in, that pull can suck the water right out of a trap, which is called siphoning. HUD’s inspection guide puts the vent’s job in one line: vents equalize the air pressure in the drainage system to prevent siphoning. HUD’s manufactured home standard requires every fixture trap to be protected against siphonage and back pressure.

Vents also let sewer gas out above the roof, where it can drift away, and they keep the drains flowing. The Union Sanitary District in California notes that when a vent is blocked, air can’t move and drains won’t work correctly. A vent through the roof has to stay open. HUD’s inspection guide says vents should be high enough above the roof that snow can’t close them, and HUD’s manufactured home standard sets a minimum of 2 inches above the roof.

The trap can’t be too far from its vent, either, or the trap arm itself can run full and siphon. HUD’s standard for manufactured homes sets these limits; your local code has its own table.

blocks.h: How a trap loses its seal
blocks.html:
• Siphoning. A full pipe flowing past, or the fixture’s own rush of water, pulls the seal out when the vent can’t supply air.
  • Back pressure. A surge of air pushed ahead of water in the stack can blow the seal up into the fixture.
  • Evaporation. In a drain nobody uses, such as a basement floor drain or a guest shower, the water slowly evaporates. The Union Sanitary District suggests running a little water into each trap every month.

HUD’s inspection guide gives an inspector’s test: run several fixtures and watch the trap water. If it moves more than an inch, the venting is probably inadequate or blocked.

blocks.h: You can refill a dry trap
blocks.html: A sewer smell from a drain you rarely use is often just a dry trap. Run water into it for a few seconds. If the smell keeps coming back, or comes from a drain that’s used every day, the vent or the drain needs a plumber’s look (Lesson 11).

blocks.h: Stacks, the building drain and the sewer
blocks.html:
Branch drains from each fixture run to a vertical pipe called a stack. A stack that carries toilet waste is a soil stack. At the bottom, the stack turns into the building drain, which the Army manual defines as the pipe that receives the waste from within the building. Just outside the foundation it becomes the building sewer (the Army manual calls it the house sewer), which runs to the public sewer main or a septic tank. Above the highest fixture, the stack keeps going up through the roof as a vent.

Drains turn corners with gentle fittings, such as wyes and sanitary tees, so waste doesn’t slam into a wall of pipe and stop. And every system needs cleanouts: capped openings where a plumber can run a cable. HUD’s inspection guide says to put them near where the main vertical drains join the building drain.

blocks.html:
EPA’s SepticSmart program explains the conventional system step by step. All the water from the house runs out one main drain pipe into a septic tank: a buried, watertight container, usually concrete, fiberglass or polyethylene. Solids sink to the bottom as sludge; oils and grease float to the top as scum. Compartments and a T-shaped outlet keep the sludge and scum in the tank, and the partly treated liquid, called effluent, flows out to the drainfield. That’s a shallow, covered excavation in unsaturated soil. The soil accepts, treats and disperses the effluent as it soaks through, removing harmful bacteria, viruses and nutrients. Send too much water to a drainfield and it can flood, with sewage coming up to the surface.

EPA’s care rules: have a typical household system inspected at least every three years by a septic service professional, and expect the tank to be pumped every three to five years. Flush only human waste and toilet paper. Avoid chemical drain openers. Don’t park or drive on the drainfield, keep trees at a distance, and send roof drains and sump pumps away from it.

lessons.title: Fixtures and How They Work
lessons.short: Toilets and the siphon flush, faucet valves, anti-scald shower valves, sinks and tubs, and washer and dishwasher hookups.
lessons.intro: Fixtures are where you meet the plumbing. A toilet is a little machine built from a float, a valve and a siphon. A faucet is a valve you can grab. A shower valve quietly protects you from scalding. Once you know how they work, most of their problems make sense.

blocks.h: The toilet: a float, a valve and a siphon
blocks.html:
The tank holds the water for the next flush. Push the handle and a lever and chain lift the flapper, a rubber plug over the flush valve at the bottom of the tank. EPA describes the flapper as the part that controls the flow of water to the bowl. Tank water rushes down into the bowl, through holes under the rim and often through a jet near the bottom.

The bowl drains through the trapway, a curved passage molded into the toilet that rises before it falls. Normally water sits in the bowl up to the top of that hump, which makes the toilet’s own trap. When the rush of water from the tank fills the trapway, it starts a siphon. The water going down the long side is heavier than the water coming up the short side, so the pressure at the top of the bend drops below the air pressure on the bowl, and the bowl empties fast. When the bowl is nearly empty, air gets in and breaks the siphon. That’s the gurgle at the end of a flush.

Meanwhile the tank refills. As its water level drops, a float drops too and opens the fill valve. Fresh water flows in, and a small refill tube sends some of it down the overflow tube to top up the bowl and restore the trap seal. The float rises with the water, held up by the buoyant force that OpenStax’s physics text describes (Archimedes’ principle), and at the set level it closes the valve. The overflow tube is a safety outlet: if the fill valve fails to shut off, water spills into the bowl instead of onto the floor.

blocks.cap: Press the handle to flush, then try the faults. The tank and bowl volumes follow the gallons per flush you pick; the timing is sped up for a clear view.

blocks.html:
EPA says older, inefficient toilets can use as much as 6 gallons per flush. The current federal standard is 1.6 gallons, and WaterSense labeled toilets use 1.28 gallons or less while passing tests for how well they clear the bowl. Toilets account for nearly 30 percent of an average home’s indoor water use, and EPA estimates that replacing old toilets with WaterSense models can save a home nearly 13,000 gallons a year.

Flappers wear out. EPA suggests replacing yours at least once every five years. If a toilet runs or refills by itself, Fix a Running Toilet walks you through the dye test, the chain and the float.

Every faucet is a valve that opens a path for water and closes it off again. Older two-handle faucets often use a compression valve: turning the handle screws a stem down until a rubber washer presses onto a metal seat. These take several turns to close, and a worn washer lets the faucet drip. EPA’s WaterSense pages note that leaky faucets can often be fixed by checking the washers and gaskets and replacing worn ones.

Most newer faucets are washerless. A cartridge faucet slides or turns a cylinder with openings in it; O-rings make the seal. A ball faucet uses a slotted ball under a single handle, with springs and rubber seats. A ceramic disc faucet uses two hard, polished discs with holes; turning the handle slides one over the other, and water flows where the holes line up. A quarter turn takes it from off to full.

At the tip of most faucets is an aerator, a small screen that mixes air into the stream. A clogged aerator can make a faucet’s stream weak, and EPA lists cleaning it regularly among its steps for reducing lead in tap water (Lesson 7).

blocks.html:
A shower valve mixes hot and cold. The danger is a sudden change: someone flushes a toilet, the cold side’s pressure drops, and the mix turns scalding. Two kinds of valve guard against that. A pressure-balancing valve has a spool that senses the hot and cold pressures and cuts back the hot when the cold drops. A thermostatic valve senses the temperature of the mixed water itself and adjusts to hold it steady.

HUD’s standard for manufactured homes requires shower and tub-shower valves to be pressure-balancing, thermostatic or a combination, with the limit stop set to no more than 120°F. The CDC adds that if a water heater is set above 120°F, thermostatic mixing valves at faucets and showers help prevent scalding (Lesson 5). Your local code sets the rules where you live.

blocks.html: Under a sink, a straight pipe called the tailpiece drops from the drain into the trap. Most bathroom sinks and tubs also have an overflow: a hole near the rim that lets water escape down the drain before it spills. That’s why you plug the overflow with a wet rag before plunging a sink; otherwise the push escapes through it instead of reaching the clog (Unclog a Sink or Toilet). Tubs work the same way, with a stopper linkage behind the overflow plate.

A dishwasher and a clothes washer each have a supply line, a shutoff valve and a drain. Their supply connections must be protected from backflow; HUD’s manufactured home standard, for example, requires a fixed air gap built into the appliance. The drain hose from a clothes washer usually hooks into a standpipe, a pipe open at the top with its own trap below, so the washer’s pump can dump water fast without siphoning the trap or letting sewer gas out. Quick-closing appliance valves are a common cause of water hammer (Lesson 9).

• Do the toilet dye test and replace a worn flapper (Fix a Running Toilet).
  • Unscrew and clean a faucet aerator or a showerhead with scale on it; EPA suggests white vinegar or a cleaning product.
  • Close a fixture’s shutoff valve before you work on it, and open a faucet to let the pressure out.

Valves inside the wall, such as a shower valve, and anything that means opening a wall or cutting into supply or drain pipes. A permit and inspection may be required, and the work may need a licensed plumber where you live.

lessons.title: Water Heaters
lessons.short: Tank heaters part by part, the temperature-and-pressure relief valve, what temperature to use, sediment, tankless and heat pump heaters.
lessons.intro: Water heating is the second-largest energy expense in the average American home, according to the Department of Energy. A tank heater is simple inside, but it holds a lot of hot water under pressure, so it has one safety part everyone should understand: the temperature-and-pressure relief valve.

blocks.h: How a tank water heater works
blocks.html:
The Department of Energy describes a conventional storage water heater as a tank holding 20 to 80 gallons for a single-family home, fueled by natural gas, propane, fuel oil or electricity. When you open a hot tap, hot water leaves from the top of the tank. Cold water enters at the bottom through the dip tube, a pipe that carries it down past the hot water, and gets heated there, so the tank always stays full.

Hot water is less dense than cold, so it floats on top. A good tank keeps that layering: hot at the top, where it leaves, and incoming cold at the bottom, where the heat goes in. A gas heater has a burner under the tank and a flue pipe up through its middle; the hot exhaust gives up heat to the water on its way out and then leaves through a draft hood and a vent. An electric heater has heating elements reaching into the water, usually an upper and a lower one, each with its own thermostat; CPSC’s scald guide mentions both behind their access panels.

A tank loses heat to the room all day, even when nobody uses hot water. That’s called standby loss, and gas and oil heaters also lose heat up the vent. Heat traps on the pipes keep warm water from rising out of the tank when it isn’t in use, according to the University of Maryland Extension.

blocks.cap: Run a hot tap and watch cold water come in through the dip tube. Pick gas or electric, try each thermostat setting, and switch to the tankless calculator to see how much power instant hot water takes.
Tank water heater parts
rows: Tank
Holds the water; insulation around it slows the heat loss.
Water around the base from the tank itself: HUD says a leaking tank usually can’t be repaired.
Dip tube
Carries incoming cold water to the bottom of the tank.
If it breaks, cold water mixes in near the top and hot water runs out fast.
Burner or elements

No hot water or not enough.
Thermostat
Turns the heat on and off to hold the set temperature.
Water too hot or not hot enough.
Anode rod
A metal rod that corrodes so the tank doesn’t; DOE suggests inspecting it every three to four years.
Once it’s used up, the tank itself starts to corrode.
T&P relief valve
Opens to release water if the temperature or pressure gets too high.

Flue, draft hood and vent (gas)
Carry exhaust, including carbon monoxide, outside.

blocks.html:
Water expands when it’s heated. OpenStax lists its coefficient of volume expansion as 210 × 10⁻⁶ per degree Celsius near room temperature, so 40 gallons heated by 70°F (39°C) grow by about a third of a gallon, and more than that in practice, because hot water expands faster. Water barely compresses, so in a closed tank that extra volume has to go somewhere, and the pressure climbs. If a thermostat failed and the heat stayed on, the temperature and pressure would keep rising.

The temperature-and-pressure relief valve, or T&P valve, is the last line of defense. The University of Maryland Extension calls it a critical safety feature that releases hot water or steam if pressure or temperature builds up too far. HUD’s inspection guide says it belongs on top of the tank or on the hot water line, not the cold. Its discharge pipe runs down to a few inches above the floor, to a floor drain, or outside, depending on local code, so the scalding water goes where it can’t hurt anyone.

HUD’s inspection standard for the housing it oversees treats a problem with this valve as a severe deficiency to fix within 24 hours: a valve that’s blocked so it can’t open fully, or a discharge pipe that is damaged, capped, slopes upward or is made of an unsuitable material. HUD’s reason is the risk of a rupturing water heater. A missing or misplaced discharge pipe is flagged too, for the risk of burns.

blocks.h: Never cap, plug or block the T&P valve or its pipe
blocks.html: Water dripping from the discharge pipe is a symptom, not a nuisance to stop. It means the valve opened because of high temperature or pressure, or that the valve is worn. Have a plumber find out which. Testing the valve releases scalding water, and HUD’s guide warns that an old valve may stick open afterward, so have a replacement on hand or leave the test to a pro. EPA suggests checking the valve at least once a year and DOE every six months; follow your heater’s manual.

Here the agencies weigh two risks: scalding and germs.

  • Energy and scalding (DOE). Some manufacturers set thermostats at 140°F, but most households need only 120°F, which DOE calls safe for most of the population. A heater kept at 140°F can waste $36 to $61 a year in standby losses, and it significantly increases the risk of scalding. DOE adds that people with a suppressed immune system or chronic respiratory disease may consider keeping the tank at 140°F, with mixing valves on the taps used for washing and bathing.
  • Scalds (CPSC). The Consumer Product Safety Commission urges setting water heaters to 120°F. Most tap water scald injuries and deaths happen to older adults and children under five. At 140°F, burns can happen in six seconds; at 130°F, in thirty seconds; even at 120°F, five minutes can cause third-degree burns.
  • Germs (CDC). Legionella, the bacteria behind Legionnaires’ disease, grow best between 77 and 113°F and spread when people breathe in mist from showers and faucets. The CDC says to set water heaters at or above 120°F to minimize its growth. Water at 130 to 140°F kills many harmful germs but raises the scalding risk, so if a heater is set above 120°F, the CDC advises thermostatic mixing valves at faucets and showers.

To check your temperature, CPSC suggests holding a candy or meat thermometer under a hot faucet, first thing in the morning or at least two hours after hot water was last used. Thermostats on gas heaters vary, so CPSC says to follow the manufacturer’s instructions or call the gas company. Electric heaters have thermostats behind panels near live wiring, and CPSC’s instructions start with switching off the power at the breaker.

blocks.html:
When hard water is heated, calcium carbonate comes out as solid deposits, the U.S. Geological Survey explains, and that scale lowers the efficiency of electric water heaters and raises the cost of heating water. Some sediment and rust collect at the bottom of every tank. A thick layer of it can make a heater rumble or pop as the water under it boils in little bursts.

Advice on flushing varies. DOE’s Energy Saver guide suggests draining a quart from the tank every three months; EPA’s checklist says to flush the heater once a year; the University of Maryland Extension says once or twice a year, especially where water is hard. Follow your heater’s manual. Drained water is scalding hot, and an old drain valve may not reseal, so many people have a plumber do it with the yearly checkup EPA suggests.

A tankless, or on-demand, water heater has no tank. The Department of Energy describes the parts of a gas unit: a high-powered burner, a fan and a heat exchanger. When a tap opens, a sensor detects the flow and starts the burner, which raises the water to a set temperature; when the tap closes, it shuts off. With no tank, there’s no standby loss. DOE says high-efficiency models can typically deliver 2 to 5 gallons per minute and that tankless heaters are 24 to 34 percent more efficient for homes using 41 gallons or less of hot water a day, or 8 to 14 percent for homes using about 86 gallons a day.

The catch is power. Heating water as fast as it flows takes a lot of it. OpenStax gives the heat needed as Q = mcΔT, with water’s specific heat at 4,186 joules per kilogram per degree Celsius. Two gallons a minute is about 0.126 kilograms each second. Warming that by 60°F (33.3°C) takes about 17.6 kilowatts, or about 60,000 Btu per hour, steadily, for as long as the shower runs. That’s why the University of Maryland Extension notes that tankless heaters often need electrical or gas upgrades.

power = flow × specific heat × temperature rise  (P = ṁ c ΔT)
0.126 kg/s × 4,186 J/(kg·°C) × 33.3°C ≈ 17,600 W ≈ 60,000 Btu/h

A heat pump water heater doesn’t make heat; it moves it. DOE compares it to a refrigerator running in reverse: it pulls heat from the surrounding air and pumps it into the water in a tank. That makes it two to three times more energy efficient than a conventional electric resistance water heater, and DOE’s guide says an ENERGY STAR model uses 70 percent less electricity for the same hot water.

It needs the right spot. DOE says the space should stay between 40 and 90°F year-round and have at least 1,000 cubic feet of air around the heater, and since it takes heat from the room, it tends to cool the space it’s in. The Science Lab explains how heat pumps move heat uphill (Engines, Refrigerators and Heat Pumps).

blocks.h: Leave installation to a qualified pro
blocks.html: DOE recommends a qualified plumbing and heating contractor to install a storage water heater, because proper installation depends on fuel type, climate, local building codes and safety, especially the combustion safety of gas- and oil-fired units. A water heater usually needs a permit. A gas heater’s vent carries carbon monoxide outdoors, and HUD treats a blocked, misaligned or missing flue as life-threatening (Lesson 10).

quiz.q: What should you never do to a T&P valve’s discharge pipe?
opts: Make it of an approved material

quiz.q: According to CPSC, how fast can 140°F tap water cause a burn?
quiz.why: Six seconds. At 130°F, thirty seconds; at 120°F, five minutes can cause third-degree burns.

quiz.q: In what range does the CDC say Legionella grows best?
quiz.why: 77 to 113°F, which is why the CDC says to keep water heaters at or above 120°F.

lessons.title: Pipes, Fittings and Joining
lessons.short: Copper, PEX, CPVC, PVC, ABS, cast iron and galvanized steel; how soldered, threaded, solvent-welded, crimped and push-fit joints work; lead-free rules.
lessons.intro: Walk into a hardware store’s plumbing aisle and you’ll see a dozen kinds of pipe and a hundred fittings. They sort out quickly once you know two things: what each pipe is for, and how its joints are made to hold water.

blocks.h: Supply pipe: what carries water under pressure
blocks.html:
• Copper. Rigid copper tube, joined by soldering, has been the standard in much of the country for decades; HUD’s inspection guide says copper came into wide use in the 1930s and normally lasts 50 years or more. It comes in wall thicknesses called types K, L and M, all named in HUD’s manufactured home standard, with K the thickest.
  • PEX (cross-linked polyethylene). Flexible plastic tubing for hot and cold water, often red and blue. It bends around corners, so it needs fewer fittings, and it’s the usual tubing for manifold systems that give each fixture its own line.
  • CPVC (chlorinated polyvinyl chloride). A rigid, cream-colored plastic rated for hot and cold water, joined with solvent cement.
  • Galvanized steel. Steel pipe coated with zinc and joined with threads, common in older homes. HUD’s inspection guide gives it a service life of 20 to 50 years; rust and mineral deposits slowly close it off from the inside, and rust-colored water, especially from hot taps, signals advanced decay.
  • Lead. Found in very old service lines and plumbing. HUD notes it may be a health hazard; Lesson 7 has EPA’s advice.

Any plastic used for drinking water must be made for it. HUD’s standard, for example, requires plastic water piping in manufactured homes to be listed for use with hot water and plastics not covered by its listed standards to be certified as non-toxic.

blocks.h: Drain pipe: what carries waste by gravity
blocks.html:
• PVC and ABS. White PVC and black ABS plastic pipe are the most familiar drain, waste and vent pipes today. HUD lists both, in Schedule 40 DWV grades. Each has its own solvent cement.
  • Cast iron. Heavy and quiet, used for stacks and building drains, especially in older homes. Older cast iron was joined at bell-shaped hubs; hubless (no-hub) pipe is joined with rubber sleeves clamped by stainless steel bands.
  • Copper DWV. A thin-walled copper tube made for drains, found in some homes.
  • Galvanized steel. Older drains and vents; it rusts and clogs over time.

HUD’s inspection guide says properly installed plastic pipe, supported and protected from sunlight, should last indefinitely, but some local codes restrict where plastic may be used. Your code decides which materials are allowed in your home.

blocks.html:
Every joint has to stay sealed against full water pressure, or against sewage, for decades.

  • Soldered (“sweated”) copper. The pipe end and fitting are cleaned bright, coated with flux, slipped together and heated; melted solder is drawn into the thin gap and fills it. HUD’s standard spells out the basics: approved solder-type fittings, surfaces cleaned bright, a noncorrosive paste flux, and for drinking water, solder with no more than 0.2 percent lead.
  • Threaded. Tapered pipe threads wedge tighter as they’re turned. A sealing compound or thread tape fills the gaps. HUD’s standard says joint compound goes on the male threads only, threads must be fully engaged, and threads may not be wrapped with string, paper or putty.
  • Solvent-welded plastic. PVC, CPVC and ABS aren’t glued so much as fused. A primer and solvent cement soften the surfaces of the pipe and the fitting, and when they’re pushed together the plastics blend and harden into one piece. Each plastic needs its own cement; HUD’s standard says to follow the manufacturer’s methods.
  • Crimp, clamp or expansion (PEX). PEX slides over a barbed fitting and a metal ring is crimped tight around it, or the tubing is expanded with a tool, slipped over the fitting, and shrinks back to grip it. Each method needs its own matched fittings and tools.
  • Push-fit. Teeth inside the fitting grip the pipe and an O-ring seals it. Quick and handy for repairs, as long as the pipe is cut square, deburred and pushed in all the way.
  • Compression and flare. A compression nut squeezes a brass ring onto the pipe; a flare fitting clamps a flared tube end. Common on fixture supply valves. HUD calls for a proper flaring tool for flared copper joints.
  • No-hub couplings. A rubber sleeve over two cast iron or plastic drain pipe ends, clamped with stainless steel bands.

blocks.html:
Lead used to be common in solder, brass and even pipe. The Safe Drinking Water Act changed that. EPA explains that the 1986 amendments banned the use of any pipe, fitting, fixture, solder or flux that wasn’t “lead free” in drinking water systems after June 1986. Back then, “lead free” meant solder and flux with no more than 0.2 percent lead and pipes with no more than 8 percent. The Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act of 2011 tightened the definition to a weighted average of 0.25 percent lead on the surfaces that touch water.

Some products are exempt because they don’t carry drinking water, including toilets, bidets, urinals, fill valves, flushometer valves, tub fillers, shower valves and service saddles, and plumbing used only for non-drinking water. That’s why you’ll see “lead free” or a certification mark on faucets and fittings meant for drinking water.

When two different metals touch in water, one can corrode the other, an effect called galvanic corrosion. HUD’s inspection guide says to separate dissimilar metal pipes with a dielectric coupling, and calls mixed galvanized steel and copper or brass piping a sign of potential trouble. No separation is needed between metal and plastic.

A homeowner’s kit covers most first jobs: adjustable wrenches, tongue-and-groove pliers, a basin wrench for faucet nuts under a sink, a tubing cutter, a deburring tool, thread tape, a flashlight, a bucket and rags, a cup plunger and a flange plunger, and a hand drain snake. Plumbers add pipe wrenches, PEX crimp or expansion tools, press tools, a torch and soldering kit, drain machines and cameras, test gauges and pipe threaders. Lesson 12 has a full starter kit.

Soldering means an open flame near wood framing and insulation, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics lists burns from hot pipes and soldering equipment among plumbers’ common injuries. Cutting into walls risks hitting wires, gas lines and pipes. Learn these skills from a pro, and check whether your work needs a permit or a licensed plumber.

lessons.title: Water Quality and Safety
lessons.short: Lead and lead service lines, testing private wells, hard water and softeners, certified filters, germs that grow in plumbing, and cross-connections.
lessons.intro: Plumbing doesn’t just move water; it can change it. Old pipes can add lead, a warm water heater can grow germs, and a well can pick up whatever is in the ground. Here’s what the health agencies say to watch for, and what to do.

blocks.html:
EPA is blunt about lead: there is no known safe level of lead in a child’s blood, and the health goal for lead in drinking water is zero. Children six and younger are the most susceptible.

Lead usually gets into water from the plumbing, not the source. EPA explains that lead enters drinking water when plumbing materials that contain it corrode. Where a home has a lead service line, the pipe from the main to the house, that line is typically the most significant source. Lead pipes are more likely in older cities and in homes built before 1986. In homes without a lead service line, the most common problems are brass or chrome-plated brass faucets and plumbing with lead solder.

blocks.h: What EPA says you can do
blocks.html:
• Find out what your service line is made of. Ask your water utility, or a licensed plumber. EPA’s Protect Your Tap guide walks you through a quick check where the line enters the house, using a coin or key and a magnet.
  • Run your water to flush the pipes before drinking, especially after it has sat for hours.
  • Use only cold water for drinking, cooking and making baby formula. Boiling water does not remove lead.
  • Use a filter certified to remove lead. EPA’s consumer tool points to filters certified for lead reduction against both NSF/ANSI Standards 53 and 42.
  • Clean your faucet’s aerator regularly.
  • Test. Testing is the only way to confirm whether lead is in your water. Use a certified laboratory and follow its sampling directions; EPA puts the cost at roughly $15 to $100.

Public water systems have to act when lead levels are high: under EPA’s rules, if more than 10 percent of tap water samples exceed the action level of 15 parts per billion, the system must take additional steps.

blocks.h: Lead service lines are a job for the utility and licensed pros
blocks.html: Replacing a service line means digging to the main, working on the utility’s side of the line and following its rules. Call your water utility first; EPA says the utility or a licensed plumber can help you find out what your line is made of. Don’t sand, cut or disturb old lead pipe yourself.

About 87 percent of Americans get water from a public supply, USGS says; most of the rest drink from private wells. EPA’s drinking water rules don’t apply to private wells, and the CDC notes that government officials do not regulate, treat or monitor them, so the owner is responsible for the water’s safety.

The CDC says to test your well water at least once each year for total coliform bacteria, nitrates, total dissolved solids and pH, and to ask your health department about other germs or chemicals common in your area. Test more often if there are problems nearby such as flooding, land disturbances or waste disposal sites; if you repair or replace part of the well system; if the water’s taste, color or smell changes; or if someone in the home becomes pregnant or a child comes to live with you. Use a state-certified laboratory.

EPA adds a few habits: keep a well cap or sanitary seal on the well, don’t cut the casing off below the ground, inspect the casing for cracks, and keep hazardous chemicals out of septic systems.

USGS defines water hardness as the amount of dissolved calcium and magnesium in the water. It’s measured in milligrams per liter as calcium carbonate: 0 to 60 is soft, 61 to 120 moderately hard, 121 to 180 hard, and more than 180 very hard. Hardness isn’t a health concern, USGS says, but it is a nuisance. Soap reacts with the calcium to form soap scum, and when hard water is heated, calcium carbonate deposits form. That scale can shorten the life of equipment, raise the cost of heating water, lower the efficiency of electric water heaters and clog pipes.

A water softener trades the hardness away. EPA explains that a cation exchange softener removes calcium and magnesium ions by exchanging them for sodium (or potassium) ions, then periodically flushes the captured ions out and recharges with salt. That regeneration can use 25 gallons of water or more a day, up to 10,000 gallons a year, and EPA’s WaterSense program decided not to label softeners, citing concerns about how the salty discharge affects wastewater treatment.

blocks.html:
A filter is only as good as its certification and its upkeep. The CDC suggests checking that a filter is certified to the standard for what you want removed, such as NSF/ANSI Standard 42 for taste and odor, Standard 53 for health-related contaminants such as cysts and lead, Standard 58 for reverse osmosis and Standard 62 for distillation. NSF International, an independent organization, keeps a database of certified products.

The CDC also points out the limits. Most home filters, like pitcher and refrigerator filters, are not designed to remove germs. Point-of-use filters treat water at one tap, usually the kitchen sink; point-of-entry, or whole-home, filters treat all the water coming in, and if a whole-home filter removes the chlorine your utility adds, more germs may grow in your plumbing. Change cartridges on the manufacturer’s schedule; a neglected filter can grow germs of its own.

blocks.html: Some bacteria live in building plumbing itself. The best known is Legionella, which causes Legionnaires’ disease. The CDC says it grows best in water between 77 and 113°F and in slowly moving or stagnant water, and people get sick by breathing in small droplets, such as shower mist. The CDC’s steps for homes and rentals: keep the water heater at or above 120°F, flush faucets and showerheads that haven’t been used for a week or more, and flush the water heater as its manufacturer recommends (Lesson 5 weighs this against scalding).

EPA defines a cross-connection as a point in a plumbing system where something that isn’t drinking water could come into contact with the drinking water. A garden hose lying in a bucket of weed killer, a hose in a pool, or a sprayer on a utility sink are all cross-connections. If pressure in the main drops, as during a main break or heavy hydrant use, water can be pulled backward through them. That’s why codes require backflow devices such as hose-bibb vacuum breakers and air gaps (Lesson 2), and why you should never leave a hose end sitting in a bucket, pool or chemical.

lessons.title: Leaks and Water Use
lessons.short: How much leaks waste, the two-hour meter test and the toilet dye test, finding hidden leaks, and reading your water bill.
lessons.intro: A drip doesn’t look like much. But EPA says the average household’s leaks can waste more than 9,300 gallons a year, and nationwide household leaks waste nearly a trillion gallons. Finding them takes two free tests and a little detective work.

blocks.html:
EPA’s WaterSense program has the numbers:

  • The average household’s leaks can waste more than 9,300 gallons a year.
  • Nine percent of homes have leaks that waste 50 gallons or more a day.
  • A faucet dripping once a second can waste more than 3,000 gallons a year.
  • A showerhead leaking 10 drips a minute wastes more than 500 gallons a year.
  • A worn toilet flapper can silently leak thousands of gallons a year, and EPA’s septic program says a single running toilet can waste up to 200 gallons a day.
  • Fixing easily corrected leaks can save about 10 percent on water bills.

The counter below turns drips into gallons and dollars. EPA’s two faucet and showerhead figures both work out to drops of about 0.36 milliliter, so that’s where the drop size starts.

blocks.cap: Set your own water price from your bill. Drop size varies with the faucet; the default matches EPA’s figures.

blocks.html:
gallons per year = drips per minute × 525,600 minutes × drop size (mL) ÷ 3,785.4 mL per gallon
60 drips/min × 525,600 × 0.36 mL ÷ 3,785.4 ≈ 3,000 gallons

Your water meter is the best leak detector you have. EPA says it’s usually underground near the curb, though it may be indoors, such as in a basement. Read it, use no water at all for two hours, and read it again. If the reading changed at all, you probably have a leak somewhere.

Your winter bill is another clue. EPA says a family of four that uses more than 12,000 gallons a month in winter, when there’s no outdoor watering, probably has a serious leak. Bills often measure water in hundreds of cubic feet, or CCF. A cubic foot is exactly 0.3048 meter cubed and a gallon is 3.785412 liters, so one CCF is about 748 gallons, and EPA’s 12,000 gallons is about 16 CCF. A bill much higher than the same month last year can also point to a leak you haven’t found.

blocks.html: 1 CCF = 100 ft³ × 28.317 L per ft³ ÷ 3.785 L per gallon ≈ 748 gallons

Toilets are common silent leakers. EPA’s test: put a few drops of food coloring or a dye tablet in the tank, don’t flush, and wait 10 minutes. If color shows up in the bowl, water is leaking past the flapper. Flush afterward so the dye doesn’t stain. EPA suggests replacing flappers at least once every five years. Fix a Running Toilet covers the fixes, and Lesson 4 has an animated toilet with the common faults.

If the meter says there’s a leak and the toilets pass the dye test, go hunting:

  • Under sinks and behind appliances: look for drips at pipe connections, puddles and water spots, as EPA suggests. Check supply lines to toilets, faucets, the dishwasher, the refrigerator ice maker and the clothes washer.
  • Faucets and showerheads: EPA notes that leaky faucets can often be fixed by replacing worn washers and gaskets, and a dripping showerhead by tightening its connection with pipe tape and a wrench.
  • The water heater: look for leaks, aged gaskets, loose connections and corrosion, and water at the T&P valve’s discharge pipe.
  • Outdoors: check the garden hose connection and its rubber washer. EPA’s older leak guide says an irrigation leak only 1/32 of an inch across can waste about 6,300 gallons a month.
  • Ceilings, walls and floors: stains, bubbling paint, warped flooring and musty smells can mark a leak inside a wall or ceiling.

EPA’s campus guide suggests a simple measurement: set a container under a drip for an hour and see how much it holds. Then you know your real leak rate.

blocks.h: Where the water goes, and using less
blocks.html: Toilets are nearly 30 percent of an average home’s indoor water use and showering nearly 17 percent, according to EPA. EPA’s septic program puts typical indoor use as high as 70 gallons per person per day in a single-family home. WaterSense labeled fixtures are independently certified to use less while still working well: EPA estimates a family can save nearly 13,000 gallons a year by replacing old toilets, 2,700 gallons a year with WaterSense showerheads and 700 gallons a year with WaterSense bathroom faucets.

lessons.title: Clogs, Frozen Pipes and Noisy Pipes
lessons.short: Why drains clog and how plungers and snakes clear them, why pipes burst in the cold, low pressure, and water hammer.
lessons.intro: Most plumbing calls come down to a handful of everyday problems: a drain that won’t drain, a pipe that froze, pressure that dropped, or pipes that bang. Each has a simple bit of physics behind it.

blocks.html:
Drains are built to carry water, human waste and toilet paper, not much else. Kitchen drains clog with grease, which cools and sticks to the pipe walls, plus food scraps. Bathroom drains clog with hair and soap. Toilets clog with too much paper or things that should never be flushed. EPA’s septic program puts the rule simply: flush only human waste and toilet paper. Wipes, grease and similar items clog pipes and septic systems.

Many clogs form close to the fixture, in or near the trap, where a plunger or a hand snake can reach them.

A plunger works because water barely compresses. Push on the cup and the push travels through the water to the clog; that’s Pascal’s principle, the same physics as a car’s brakes. Pulling back tugs the other way, rocking the clog loose. The cup needs water over it to seal, and other openings, such as a sink’s overflow, must be plugged so the push doesn’t escape. Use a cup plunger on sinks and tubs and a flange plunger, with its extra rubber sleeve, on toilets (Unclog a Sink or Toilet).

If plunging fails, a hand drain snake, or auger, is a coiled steel cable you crank into the drain to hook or break up the clog. For clogs deep in the building drain or sewer, plumbers use powered drain machines through a cleanout, and cameras to see what’s down there.

blocks.html: EPA’s septic program advises avoiding chemical drain openers. Never mix drain cleaners or other products, and don’t plunge a drain that has chemical cleaner in it; call a plumber instead. If water backs up in more than one place, such as a tub when the toilet flushes, the clog is probably farther down the line: stop using water and call a plumber.

Water is strange: it expands when it freezes. USGS says ice is about 9 percent less dense than water, so a given amount of water needs about 9 percent more room as ice. In a pipe, an ice plug forms first where the pipe is coldest. The water trapped between the ice and a closed faucet has nowhere to go as the ice grows, and the pressure soars until the pipe splits. That’s why pipes often burst a short distance from the ice, and why a split may not leak until it thaws.

Pipes most at risk run through cold spaces: outside walls, crawlspaces, attics, garages and unheated basements, plus outdoor hose bibbs and sprinkler lines.

blocks.html:
• Insulate and protect. HUD’s standard for manufactured homes requires all piping exposed to freezing temperatures to be insulated or protected; where heat tape or pipe heating cable is used, it must be listed for that purpose. The Department of Energy recommends insulating pipes that must run in exterior walls, putting cavity insulation behind them, and sealing the wall cavity so cold air can’t flow around them.
  • Drain outdoor lines. EPA says to shut off the water to irrigation systems and drain the lines before freezing weather.
  • Turn off hose bibbs when you aren’t using them, as EPA’s checklist suggests, and disconnect hoses in winter.
  • Know your main shutoff. If a pipe bursts, close the main valve right away (Shut Off Your Home’s Water).

blocks.h: If a pipe is frozen or has burst
blocks.html: If water is spraying or a pipe has split, close the main shutoff now and call a licensed plumber. If a faucet gives only a trickle in freezing weather, a pipe may be frozen and could split as it thaws, so be ready to close the main. Thawing a frozen pipe safely depends on where it is and what it’s made of; your water utility or a plumber can advise. Never use an open flame on pipes in a wall or near framing.

Start by asking where. If one faucet or showerhead is weak, the cause is usually right there: a clogged aerator, or scale in the showerhead, which EPA says to clean with a cleaning product or white vinegar, or a fixture shutoff valve that isn’t fully open. If the whole house is weak, check that the main shutoff is fully open, ask your neighbors and your water utility, and think about the pressure-reducing valve (Lesson 2). In an older house with galvanized steel pipe, HUD’s inspection guide notes the pipes may be clogged inside by rust and mineral deposits. HUD’s gallon-jug test, about 24 seconds at the kitchen faucet, gives you a number to compare.

The U.S. Army’s plumbing manual explains water hammer: when flowing water is stopped abruptly, it slams against the valve, and the result is noise, rattling pipes and sometimes leaky joints. Toilet fill valves, washing machines and dishwashers close quickly, so the bang often comes right after one of them finishes. The fix is a cushion of air: an air chamber, a capped pipe that holds air, or a manufactured water hammer arrester, installed near the valve. San Diego’s utility guidance adds that banging or a high-pitched whistle, often when the water is turned off, can mean a failing pressure-reducing valve and too much pressure.

Other noises have other causes: a rumble or pops from a water heater often mean sediment in the tank (Lesson 5), and ticking as hot pipes warm up is the pipe expanding against its supports.

lessons.title: Gas Piping and Gas Appliances
lessons.short: How natural gas and propane reach appliances, shutoff valves and connectors, venting and carbon monoxide, why gas work is licensed, and what to do if you smell gas.
lessons.intro: Many plumbers also run the gas lines that feed water heaters, furnaces, ranges and dryers. Gas work is a different world from water: a leak isn’t a puddle, it’s a fire or explosion risk, and a bad vent can fill a house with carbon monoxide. This lesson explains how the system works and why it belongs to licensed pros. It is not a how-to.

blocks.html:
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission says that if you smell gas and suspect a leak:

  • Leave the house immediately.
  • Do not use your phone.
  • Call your gas supplier, or dial 911, from a neighbor’s house.
  • Do not light a match, turn on a light, or switch on anything electrical.

And if a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, CPSC says to get everyone outside to fresh air right away and call 911 or the fire department. Don’t go back in until the emergency responders say it’s safe.

Natural gas comes from the utility’s main through a service line to a meter, usually outside the house. Propane comes from a tank on the property. From there, house gas piping carries it to each appliance. Near each appliance is a shutoff valve so that one appliance can be turned off for service; HUD’s manufactured home standard, as an example, requires an accessible shutoff within 3 feet of most appliances and within 6 feet of a cooking appliance. A short, flexible connector joins the valve to the appliance. Then the appliance burns the gas, and a vent carries the exhaust outdoors.

Gas piping is built from materials approved for gas. HUD’s standard lists steel or wrought-iron pipe, threaded brass, certain grades of copper tubing and corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) that is listed and installed to its standard. Joints use compound that resists the gas.

blocks.html:
Household gas runs at a very low pressure compared with water. Gas pressure is often measured in inches of water column. HUD’s manufactured home standard designs the gas system for no more than 14 inches of water column and no less than 7. NIST puts an inch of water at about 249 pascals, so that’s roughly a quarter to a half of a psi, about a hundred times less than typical water pressure.

Low pressure doesn’t make a leak harmless. CPSC warns that a gas leak can cause a fire or explosion. That’s why pros pressure-test new piping before connecting appliances. HUD’s standard, for example, requires the piping to hold 3 psi for at least 10 minutes with no drop, and connections checked with soapy water or bubble solution, never a flame.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics notes that most states require plumbers to be licensed, and some require a special license for gas line work. Gas piping has to be sized so every appliance gets enough gas at once, built from listed parts, supported, protected, pressure-tested, and often inspected before it’s used. Mistakes can kill. Installing, extending, repairing or disconnecting gas piping, and installing gas appliances, belong to a licensed professional, usually with a permit.

Even small parts matter. CPSC warns that some older uncoated brass connectors can separate from their end pieces and cause a leak, fire or explosion. Its advice: have only a qualified professional check and replace a connector; don’t try it yourself, and don’t even move the appliance to look, because moving it can cause a failure.

Burning gas makes hot exhaust that has to leave the house. When burning is incomplete, it makes carbon monoxide, which CPSC describes as a deadly, colorless, odorless, poisonous gas. CPSC lists malfunctioning fuel-burning appliances, such as furnaces, ranges, water heaters and room heaters, among its sources.

HUD’s manufactured home standard requires fuel-burning appliances to be vented to the outside, except ranges and ovens. Older water heaters and furnaces use natural draft: hot flue gas rises through a draft hood and a vent pipe on its own. If that vent is blocked or disconnected, exhaust can spill into the room. HUD’s inspection standard treats a blocked, misaligned or missing flue as life-threatening because of carbon monoxide, and HUD’s inspection guide says soot on top of a water heater, under the draft hood, points to a clogged flue. Newer direct-vent, sealed-combustion appliances draw their combustion air from outdoors and send exhaust out through sealed pipes; DOE says that design makes them unlikely to backdraft.

blocks.html:
• Know where your gas meter and appliance shutoff valves are, but leave the valves to the gas company and pros unless they instruct you otherwise.
  • Follow CPSC’s advice: have heating systems professionally inspected and serviced every year, including chimneys and flues, and keep vents clear of debris.
  • Install battery-operated CO alarms, or alarms with battery backup, on every level and outside sleeping areas, and test them (Test Smoke and CO Alarms).
  • Learn what to do if you smell gas, and teach everyone in the house.

In earthquake zones, a heavy water heater can tip over and break its gas line. HUD’s inspection guide says to check for seismic bracing that ties the water heater to the floor or wall framing, to check the gas service for vulnerability where it enters the building, and in the most active zones to look for an automatic emergency gas shutoff valve for the whole house. Local codes in those areas set the requirements.

Turn on the lights to look

lessons.title: Troubleshooting by Symptom
lessons.short: An interactive finder: pick a symptom, answer a question, and get likely causes, safe checks and when to call a plumber.
lessons.intro: Good troubleshooting starts with three questions. Is it the supply or the drains? Is it one fixture or the whole house? Hot, cold, or both? The answers point to a system, and the system points to a fix. This finder walks you through the common problems.

blocks.html:
1. Supply or drain? Water that won’t come out, or comes out wrong, is a supply problem. Water that won’t go away, or smells, is a drain problem.
  2. One fixture or many? A problem at one faucet is usually at that faucet. A problem everywhere is usually at the main, the meter, the pressure-reducing valve, the water heater or the building drain.
  3. Hot, cold, or both? A hot-only problem points to the water heater or the hot lines.
  4. When did it start? After a cold night, after work on the street, after a new appliance? The timing is a clue.
  5. Know when to stop. Water spraying or pouring: close the main shutoff first (Shut Off Your Home’s Water). The smell of gas: leave the house and call from outside. Sewage backing up: stop running water. The finder marks these.

blocks.html:
• Know where your main shutoff is, and close it if water is getting where it shouldn’t.
  • Write down the symptoms: which fixtures, hot or cold, when it started, what you’ve tried.
  • Check whether the plumber is licensed where you live; the Bureau of Labor Statistics notes most states and some localities require it. Ask whether the job needs a permit.
  • Get a written estimate for anything beyond a simple repair.

quiz.q: Water is spraying from a pipe under the sink. What do you do first?
opts: Close the fixture valve or the main shutoff
Put a bucket under it and go to bed
quiz.why: Stop the water first, then deal with the repair.

quiz.q: Only the hot water has low pressure. Where would you look?
opts: The water heater and hot lines
quiz.why: A hot-only problem points to the heater, its valves or the hot piping.

quiz.q: Every drain in the house is slow and the lowest one backs up. What’s likely?
opts: A blockage in the building drain or sewer, or a full septic system
quiz.why: Many fixtures at once means a problem downstream of all of them.

lessons.title: Doing Your Own Work
lessons.short: A starter tool kit, shutting off the water first, permits and inspections, what homeowners commonly do, and the skill ladder.
lessons.intro: A lot of plumbing is within reach: clearing a clog, fixing a running toilet, cleaning an aerator, finding a leak. Some of it isn’t, by law or by risk. This lesson helps you tell the difference and build skill one rung at a time.

blocks.html:
• A flashlight or headlamp, rags, a bucket and old towels
  • A cup plunger for sinks and tubs, and a flange plunger for toilets
  • A hand drain snake (auger)
  • Two adjustable wrenches and a pair of tongue-and-groove pliers
  • A basin wrench, for nuts under a sink
  • Thread-sealing tape and a small tube of pipe joint compound
  • A water pressure gauge that threads onto a hose bibb
  • A kitchen thermometer, to check hot water temperature as CPSC suggests
  • Food coloring or dye tablets, for the toilet dye test
  • Safety glasses and gloves

Before you take anything apart, stop the water. Close the fixture’s own shutoff valve if it has one, or the main shutoff, then open a faucet to let out the leftover pressure. Have a bucket and towels ready for the water still in the pipes. If a valve is stuck or won’t close all the way, stop; forcing an old valve can break it. Shut Off Your Home’s Water shows how.

For anything on the water heater, turn off its power at the breaker or set a gas heater to its pilot or off setting as the manual describes, and let the water cool. Hot water burns quickly (Lesson 5).

Plumbing rules are set by states and local governments. A permit is the building department’s way of making sure work meets the code, and an inspection is how it checks, usually before walls are closed up. Replacing a faucet or a toilet often needs no permit; adding a bathroom, moving drains, replacing a water heater or working on gas lines often does. Some places let homeowners do permitted work on their own home; others require a licensed plumber for more of it. The Bureau of Labor Statistics notes that most states and some localities require plumbers to be licensed, and some require a special license for gas line work.

When in doubt, call your building department and ask. It’s free, and it saves money and trouble later, when you sell the house or file an insurance claim.

blocks.html: Climb one rung at a time. Do each new job with an experienced helper the first time, with the manufacturer’s instructions open. The fourth rung isn’t a challenge to work up to: those jobs need a license, special training, a permit or equipment.

Plumbing jobs have a way of growing: a stuck valve, a corroded nut, a rotten subfloor. It’s fine to stop, close the water off, and call a plumber. Leaving a job half-done with the water off is better than forcing it.

quiz.q: What’s the first step before taking apart any plumbing fixture?
opts: Shut off its water and open a faucet to relieve the pressure
quiz.why: Stop the water first, then relieve the pressure.

quiz.q: Which job belongs on the “leave it to licensed pros” rung?
quiz.why: Gas piping needs a licensed professional, and often a permit.

quiz.q: Why do inspections usually happen before walls are closed?
opts: So the inspector can see the pipes and test them
quiz.why: Once the walls are closed, the work can’t be seen or easily fixed.

quiz.q: A shutoff valve won’t turn. What should you do?
opts: Use a longer wrench and force it
Stop and call a plumber; forcing an old valve can break it
quiz.why: Old valves can snap; then you have a flood instead of a stuck valve.

lessons.title: Careers in Plumbing
lessons.short: What plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters do, how apprenticeships and licenses work, and current pay and job outlook from BLS.
lessons.intro: Every building needs water in and waste out, and somebody has to design, install and fix it. Plumbing is one of the skilled trades you can learn while you earn, through a paid apprenticeship, and it can lead to a license, a business of your own, or both.

blocks.html:
The Bureau of Labor Statistics describes plumbers as installing and repairing water, gas and other piping systems in homes, businesses and factories. They install fixtures and appliances such as water heaters, clean drains, repair broken pipes and help maintain septic systems. Pipefitters and steamfitters work on piping that carries chemicals, acids, gases and steam, often in factories and power plants. BLS lists the everyday tasks:

  • Prepare cost estimates for clients
  • Read blueprints and follow state and local building codes
  • Determine the materials and equipment needed for a job
  • Install pipes and fixtures
  • Inspect and test installed pipe systems and pipelines
  • Troubleshoot malfunctioning systems
  • Maintain and repair plumbing systems

BLS lists the important qualities: communication skills, dexterity in tight spaces, mechanical skills, physical strength and troubleshooting skills. Most work full time, including nights and weekends, and many are on call for emergencies. Common injuries include cuts from sharp tools, burns from hot pipes and soldering equipment, and falls from ladders.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Occupational Outlook Handbook (page last modified August 27, 2026), the median pay for plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters was $63,800 a year, or $30.67 an hour, in May 2025. The lowest-paid 10 percent earned less than $44,150 and the highest-paid 10 percent more than $108,420.

There were 510,600 of these jobs in 2025. Employment is projected to grow 7 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations, adding about 34,500 jobs, with about 42,000 openings a year on average. Many openings come from replacing workers who move to other jobs or retire. BLS says demand for plumbers comes from new construction and from maintaining and repairing the systems in existing buildings. These figures are updated every year; check the handbook for the latest.

blocks.html:
BLS says a high school diploma or equivalent is typically required, and most plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters learn on the job through an apprenticeship. Apprenticeships usually last 4 or 5 years. Each year, apprentices typically get 2,000 hours of paid on-the-job training plus some technical instruction, covering safety, local plumbing codes and blueprint reading, along with math, applied physics and chemistry. Unions, trade associations and businesses sponsor programs. Vocational-technical schools offer courses in pipe system design, safety and tool use.

A Registered Apprenticeship is approved and validated by the U.S. Department of Labor or a state apprenticeship agency. Apprenticeship.gov describes it as a paid job with a mentor, structured on-the-job training, supplemental classroom education, wage increases as your skills grow, and a portable, nationally recognized credential at the end. You can search for programs near you on Apprenticeship.gov.

blocks.html:
Most states and some localities require plumbers to be licensed, BLS says. Licensing often requires 2 to 5 years of experience and passing an exam on the trade and the local code. After finishing an apprenticeship and passing the licensing exam, a worker is considered journey-level. Master plumbers generally need several more years of experience and another exam; some go on to supervise, manage projects, or start their own contracting business, which may need additional licensing. Some states require pipefitters and steamfitters to be licensed too, and some require a separate license for gas line work.

The details, from the hours you need to the exam, are set by each state and sometimes each city or county. Your state’s plumbing licensing board or department of labor has them.

Plumbing skills lead to pipefitting and steamfitting, sprinkler fitting for fire protection systems, and to the neighboring trades. More courses are on The Trades page, including HVAC, where many of the same skills apply.
