opts.label: Everywhere in the house
causes: Work or a main break in the street, or a utility shutoff
Your main shutoff valve is closed or partly closed
In freezing weather, a frozen service line or pipe where it enters
With a private well: the pump, its pressure switch or its power
checks: Ask your neighbors and check with your water utility.
Make sure your main shutoff valve is fully open.
With a well, check the breaker for the well pump.
opts.stop: If a pipe may be frozen, be ready to close the main shutoff: a split pipe can start leaking as it thaws.
opts.pro: For a frozen service line or a well that won’t run, call a licensed plumber or well contractor.

opts.label: Only at one faucet or fixture
causes: The fixture’s shutoff valve is closed
A clogged aerator, cartridge or showerhead
In freezing weather, a frozen pipe in an outside wall
checks: Open the fixture’s shutoff valve fully.
Unscrew and clean the aerator or showerhead.
Think about where that pipe runs: an outside wall or crawlspace?
opts.stop: If a frozen pipe could have split, know where your main shutoff is before it thaws.
opts.pro: A plumber can thaw and repair frozen pipes and replace a worn valve or cartridge.

opts.label: Everywhere, hot and cold
causes: The main shutoff isn’t fully open
A failing pressure-reducing valve
Old galvanized pipes clogged inside with rust and minerals
A problem in the utility’s system, or a leak
checks: Open the main shutoff fully.
Ask neighbors whether their pressure is low too.
Time how long the kitchen faucet takes to fill a gallon jug; HUD’s guide says about 24 seconds is good.
Do the two-hour meter test for a hidden leak.
opts.stop: Not urgent unless it comes with water where it shouldn’t be.
opts.pro: A plumber can test the pressure, check or replace the PRV, and assess old piping.

opts.label: At one faucet or shower
causes: A clogged aerator
Scale in the showerhead
A partly closed fixture valve
A worn faucet cartridge
checks: Clean the aerator or showerhead; EPA suggests a cleaning product or white vinegar for scale.
Open the fixture shutoff fully.
opts.stop: Not urgent.
opts.pro: If cleaning doesn’t help, the valve or cartridge may need replacing.

opts.label: Only on the hot side
causes: The valve on the water heater is partly closed
Sediment or scale in the heater or hot lines
Corroded galvanized hot water pipes
checks: Check that the valve on the heater’s cold inlet is fully open.
Compare several hot taps.
opts.stop: Don’t open the heater’s drain or T&P valve to “clear it”: the water is scalding.
opts.pro: A plumber can flush the heater and check the hot piping.

finder.name: No hot water
finder.q: What kind of water heater, and what happens?

opts.label: Electric: no hot water at all
causes: A tripped circuit breaker
A failed heating element or thermostat
A tripped high-temperature cutoff
checks: Check the heater’s breaker in the panel.
If the breaker trips again, leave it off.
opts.stop: The heater’s access panels hide live wiring. CPSC’s own instructions for adjusting a thermostat start with switching off the power at the breaker.
opts.pro: Element, thermostat and cutoff problems are for a plumber or electrician.

opts.label: Gas: no hot water at all
causes: The pilot or burner is out
The gas supply to the heater is off
A safety device has shut the burner off
A venting problem
checks: Follow the lighting instructions printed on the heater’s label exactly.
Look for soot on top of the heater, a sign of a clogged flue.
opts.stop: If you smell gas, don’t light anything: leave the house and call the gas company or 911 from outside. If you see soot or the vent is disconnected, don’t use the heater.
opts.pro: Repeated outages, soot or venting problems need a licensed professional.

opts.label: Hot water runs out fast
causes: More hot water use than the tank can supply
Sediment taking up room at the bottom of the tank
A broken dip tube letting cold water mix in near the top
Thermostat set low, or one electric element failed
checks: Spread out showers, laundry and dishes.
Check the temperature at a tap with a thermometer.
opts.stop: Don’t raise the thermostat past 120°F without anti-scald protection; CPSC says 140°F water can burn in six seconds.
opts.pro: A plumber can check the dip tube, elements and sediment.

opts.label: Runs constantly; water trickles into the overflow tube
causes: The float is set too high
A worn fill valve
checks: Lower the float until the water stops below the top of the overflow tube.
Flush and watch the refill.
opts.stop: Not urgent, but a running toilet can waste up to 200 gallons a day.
opts.pro: If adjusting the float doesn’t stop it, replace the fill valve or call a plumber.

opts.label: Refills on its own every so often
causes: Water leaking past a worn flapper
A chain caught under the flapper
checks: Do the dye test: a few drops of food coloring in the tank, wait 10 minutes, look for color in the bowl.
Check the chain’s slack.
opts.stop: Not urgent. EPA suggests replacing flappers at least every five years.
opts.pro: If a new flapper doesn’t fix it, the flush valve seat may be worn.

opts.label: Won’t stop running after a flush
causes: A chain too short, holding the flapper open
A flapper that doesn’t drop back onto its seat
A sticking handle
checks: Lift the tank lid and see whether the flapper closed.
Adjust the chain to leave a little slack.
opts.stop: Close the toilet’s shutoff valve if you can’t stop it.
opts.pro: Call a plumber if the parts are broken or the toilet keeps misbehaving.

opts.label: One drain is slow
causes: Hair and soap in a tub or bathroom sink
Grease and food in a kitchen sink
A clog in the trap
checks: Plunge it, with the overflow plugged and water over the cup.
Try a hand drain snake.
opts.stop: Never mix drain cleaners, and don’t plunge a drain that already has chemical cleaner in it.
opts.pro: If plunging and a hand snake don’t clear it, call a plumber.

opts.label: It gurgles, or the trap water bubbles
causes: A blocked or missing vent
A partial clog farther down the drain
checks: Listen for gurgling at other fixtures when one drains.
From the ground, look for anything covering the roof vent; don’t climb on the roof.
opts.stop: Not urgent unless sewer smells come with it.
opts.pro: A plumber can clear the vent from the roof and check the drain.

opts.label: Several drains, or water comes up in a tub or floor drain
causes: A blockage in the building drain or sewer, such as roots
A full or failing septic system
checks: Stop running water, flushing and laundry.
If you have a septic system, note when it was last pumped.
opts.stop: Stop using water so sewage doesn’t back up into the house.
opts.pro: Call a plumber, or a septic professional if you have a septic system.

finder.name: Sewer smell
finder.q: Where does the smell come from?

opts.label: A drain that’s rarely used
causes: The trap’s water seal has evaporated
checks: Run water into the drain for a few seconds; the Union Sanitary District suggests doing it monthly.
opts.stop: Not urgent.
opts.pro: If it comes back within days, have a plumber check the trap and vent.

opts.label: Around a toilet, or from drains used every day
causes: A failed seal under the toilet
A blocked or broken vent
A cracked drain pipe or loose fitting
checks: Look for water at the toilet’s base, or a toilet that rocks.
Notice whether the smell follows draining or flushing.
opts.stop: Sewer gas shouldn’t be in the house; don’t ignore a persistent smell.
opts.pro: A plumber can reset the toilet, test the drains and check the vents.

opts.label: Outside, over the septic drainfield, with soggy ground
causes: A failing or overloaded septic drainfield
checks: Keep people and pets off the wet area.
Cut back water use.
opts.stop: Sewage on the surface is a health hazard.
opts.pro: Call a septic professional.

finder.name: Leaking water heater
finder.q: Where is the water coming from?

opts.label: From the T&P valve’s discharge pipe
causes: High temperature or pressure in the tank, so the valve opened
A worn T&P valve
checks: Note how often it drips and whether the water is hot.
opts.stop: Never cap, plug or block the valve or its pipe. HUD treats a capped discharge pipe as a severe hazard because the heater could rupture.
opts.pro: Have a plumber find out why it opened and replace the valve if needed.

opts.label: From the tank itself, pooling at the base
causes: A corroded tank
checks: Close the water to the heater, or the main shutoff, to limit the damage.
Turn off the heater’s power or gas as its manual describes.
opts.stop: HUD’s inspection guide says a leaking tank usually can’t be repaired and must be replaced.
opts.pro: A licensed plumber, with a permit where required, replaces the heater.

opts.label: From pipes or fittings on top
causes: A loose connection
A worn gasket
Corrosion at a fitting
checks: Dry the area and watch where the water appears first.
EPA suggests checking for leaks, aged gaskets, loose connections and corrosion.
opts.stop: Keep the area dry and away from electrical outlets.
opts.pro: A plumber can replace fittings or connectors.

opts.label: A bathroom
causes: A leaking tub or shower drain, or the tub overflow
A failed seal under the toilet
A leaking supply line or valve
checks: Use one fixture at a time and watch whether the stain grows.
Close that fixture’s shutoff valve.
opts.stop: If water is dripping, close the main shutoff. Stay out from under a wet, sagging ceiling.
opts.pro: A plumber can find the leak; the ceiling may need opening to dry out.

opts.label: Not a bathroom
causes: A leaking supply pipe in the ceiling or wall
Condensation dripping from cold pipes in humid weather
A roof or window leak
checks: Do the two-hour meter test: if the meter moves, it’s likely a plumbing leak.
Notice whether it’s worse after rain.
opts.stop: If water is actively dripping, close the main shutoff.
opts.pro: A plumber for pipe leaks; a roofer for roof leaks.

opts.label: A bang when a valve or appliance shuts off
causes: Water hammer from a quick-closing valve
Water pressure too high
checks: Note which fixture or appliance sets it off.
Measure your pressure with a gauge on a hose bibb.
opts.stop: Repeated hammer can loosen joints; don’t ignore it.
opts.pro: A plumber can add water hammer arresters and check the pressure-reducing valve.

opts.label: A whistle or squeal
causes: A failing pressure-reducing valve
A partly closed valve or worn washer
checks: Note whether it happens when water is turned off or while it runs.
opts.stop: Not dangerous by itself.
opts.pro: A plumber can test and replace the PRV.

opts.label: Rumbling or popping from the water heater
causes: Sediment in the bottom of the tank
checks: Follow the manual’s schedule for flushing the tank.
opts.stop: Don’t open the drain or T&P valve unless you’ve read the manual; the water is scalding.
opts.pro: A plumber can flush the tank during a yearly checkup.

opts.label: Rusty water, mostly from hot taps
causes: Corroding galvanized steel pipes
A corroding water heater tank
checks: Compare hot and cold taps.
Check whether it clears after running a minute.
opts.stop: Use cold water for drinking and cooking.
opts.pro: A plumber can tell whether it’s the heater or the pipes.

opts.label: Brown or cloudy water from every tap, suddenly
causes: Something stirred up in the public mains, or a problem in your service line
checks: Call your water utility and ask whether there is work or a problem in the area.
Ask your neighbors.
opts.stop: Follow your utility’s instructions; if it issues a boil water advisory, follow it.
opts.pro: If it’s only your house, a plumber can check the service line.

opts.label: White crust on faucets, showerheads and the kettle
causes: Hard water scale
checks: Look up your hardness in your utility’s water quality report.
opts.stop: Not a health concern, USGS says, but it builds up in heaters and pipes.
opts.pro: A water treatment pro or plumber can talk through softeners.

opts.label: A faucet gives a trickle or nothing in freezing weather
causes: A pipe frozen in an outside wall, crawlspace, attic or garage
checks: Find where that pipe runs.
Know where your main shutoff is and keep the path to it clear.
opts.stop: A split pipe may not leak until it thaws. Never use an open flame on pipes.
opts.pro: A licensed plumber can thaw and repair it safely.

opts.label: Water spraying or a pipe has split
causes: A burst pipe
checks: Close the main shutoff right away.
Open a faucet to let out the pressure.
opts.stop: Shut off the water first. Keep away from water near electrical outlets and appliances.
opts.pro: Call a licensed plumber.

finder.name: Gas smell
finder.q: Do you smell gas in or near the house?

opts.label: I smell gas
causes: A gas leak at an appliance, a connector, the piping or the meter
checks: Leave the house immediately.
Call your gas supplier or 911 from a neighbor’s house.
opts.stop: CPSC: don’t use your phone inside, don’t light a match, don’t turn on a light or switch on anything electrical.
opts.pro: The gas utility and licensed professionals find and fix gas leaks. Don’t go back in until they say it’s safe.
